Editor’s note: Many of you will have scrolled past clips of the giant spherical venue Sphere in Las Vegas, or the stunning sights and sounds inside it. In this two-part series, Dr. Jiajun Yang of Holoplot reveals the secrets of the Sphere’s acoustic design. The first part explains why acoustic design inside the Sphere is so hard; the second explains how the problems were solved.

Since it officially opened in September 2023, Madison Square Garden’s Las Vegas Sphere (MSG Sphere) has caused a sensation around the world. Even if you have not been there yourself, you have probably seen its huge exterior screen in action on social media, from the giant eyeball in aerial shots to the dazzling visual effects of U2’s concerts. It is a visual spectacle through and through.

But beyond the visuals, the core element of this spherical venue, with a footprint of 80,000 square meters and room for 20,000 spectators, is in fact sound. After all, music is the soul of the concert experience.

Image: Wikipedia

This article looks at the Sphere’s “audio colossus” from the perspective of sound control and sound system design: a vast system of more than 1,600 Holoplot X1 Matrix Array loudspeakers with more than 160,000 drivers in total, one of the largest and most complex sound reinforcement projects in the world today. We will cover:

  • why sound control matters, and the problems unique to the Sphere

  • conventional line arrays vs. wave field synthesis matrix arrays

  • moving audio data for so many drivers and channels: the basics of AES67/Ravenna networked audio

  • how to do spatial audio, or immersive surround sound, in a large venue

Sound control: why does it matter?

Before we look at the Sphere’s sound system, let’s talk about sound control at concerts. As the name suggests, it means directing sound so that it covers given areas in a controlled way, according to a set design. Ideally, we want:

  • Even coverage: every seat in the house enjoys the same level and sound quality;

  • A clear mix: clean musical detail in every area, unaffected by the building’s reverberation (unless that is intended);

  • Time alignment: wherever listeners sit, all sources reach them accurately in sync, which is also called delay compensation;

  • Stage monitoring: performers are not disturbed by the PA and can hear their wedges or in-ear monitors clearly.

But suppose you cover the venue with a single loudspeaker (a point source). Because sound spreads out spherically, even a waveguide cannot focus it into tight directivity, and the sound pressure also falls exponentially with distance. That is why the line array is the widely adopted sound-control solution today.

Image: holoplot.com. How sound spreads and decays with distance

Image: isp-audio.com. An L-Acoustics line array

How line arrays work, and their limits

A line array system stacks many loudspeaker units (drivers) vertically and precisely controls their output to form a specific radiation pattern. Its basic principles include:

  • Wavefront summation and interference
    The waves from the individual units add up; by adjusting spacing and phase, the array concentrates a beam in the target direction while controlling horizontal and vertical coverage.

  • Extended coverage and control of decay
    Many drivers working together slow the drop-off with distance, while digital delay compensation keeps the sound in sync across different areas.

  • Directivity and shaping of the radiation pattern
    By designing the array’s structure and phase relationships, side and rear radiation can be greatly reduced, keeping the main reinforcement concentrated on the audience.

Line array theory is complex, and this article cannot do it full justice. For more, I recommend “Line Array Realities” at prosoundtraining.com and “Line Arrays Explained” at soundonsound.com.

Image: holoplot.com. Horizontal and vertical sound pressure distribution of a line array

Sound control in the Sphere: harder still

A line array on its own has limitations, for example in coverage uniformity, in how far the coverage shape can be adjusted, and in how differently frequency bands decay. The Sphere’s design adds a whole series of challenges that raise the difficulty further.

1. Invisible loudspeakers

You may have noticed that there are no visible PA loudspeakers or arrays inside the Sphere. That is because one of the Sphere’s core ideas is its immersive spherical screen, and putting huge loudspeakers in the audience’s line of sight would inevitably spoil the visuals. So the loudspeakers have to be hidden, while still delivering the sound pressure level a 20,000-capacity venue needs.

Image: www.gdbarkin.com. Dead & Company live at the Sphere.

2. An architectural acoustics nightmare: the sphere

A spherical building tends to cause irregular reflections and focusing, so that sound piles up excessively in some areas and cancels in others, unbalancing the sound. Reflections from the sphere also add a great deal of reverberation, which muddies the sound. To give everyone an even, clear listening experience, the sound system has to correct and compensate for these acoustic dead spots and hot spots, and keep unnecessary reverberation to a minimum.

3. A multi-tier, theater-style layout

The venue uses a traditional theater layout with raked, multi-tier seating, so every tier needs accurate delay compensation and optimized coverage.

4. Immersive spatial audio

The Sphere sells itself on immersive shows. In a huge venue, a simple surround system easily falls into the trap where only the people in the middle get the best experience. For the whole audience to enjoy rich movement of sound images and surround effects, surround sound has to be delivered zone by zone.

5. Stage monitoring

Every stage needs clear monitoring or in-ears, so the PA must keep its sound off the stage as far as possible. But the Sphere’s screen (problem 1) makes it hard for conventional reinforcement to avoid the stage, and as the photo above shows, the audience is only a few meters from the stage. This calls for a more precise way of separating stage and audience zones.

These are the reasons acoustic design inside the Sphere is so hard. So how were the problems solved?

About the author: Jiajun Yang holds a PhD in music technology from the University of York in the UK. He went on to a postdoc in sonification with the Ambient Intelligence group at Bielefeld University in Germany, and joined Holoplot’s software team in 2020. He loves programming and audio technology, knows AES67 and Dante networked audio well, and has lately followed the crowd down the Rust rabbit hole.
